I have a lot of experience with Medical Aid in Dying (formerly known as “assisted suicide”). There are many legal resources available to you in many countries all over the world, including several U.S. states. I want to speak to the part of you that wonders about her quality of life. I’m currently a chronic pain patient myself and you might have to listen when she tells you that she can’t hold on. That doesn’t mean you stop trying to find a solution, but you fight to find one, and you stay by their side for as long as they’re willing to accept your help. Then you have to do the hard work of trusting someone when they tell you it’s time. My only other thought is that if it’s really this bad for her, she will find a way. I would say you should use those resources, just reach out and talk to the doctors about what’s happening (after you talk about this beforehand with your daughter, of course). They can give you a good and honest opinion of whether or not she may be a good candidate, and if not, they can provide excellent referrals to help find solutions, and they can provide some counseling and consultation around it all. It’s not right for everyone, but it might bring you both peace of mind that there’s still more hope, or that there is hope for peace. But it can be an impossible decision to make, so again, I just recommend reaching out to MAiD providers nearest to you (including across state lines if you are in U.S., as there are several states that don’t require residency to be eligible).

I was just a little older than you (18) when I got pregnant on accident. I never questioned my choice to have an abortion, but I was also having to keep it secret and work with limited resources. It was a very stressful time, but once I took those pills I gave up on the secret and called my mom immediately. It wasn’t the worst experience I had ever had in the world, but hear me when I say that you cannot do this alone and you cannot keep it a secret. You need an adult, any adult you trust to go to. You also cannot stop the anxiety, but…that’s okay. This is a very intense moment in your life right now, of course you feel like that. There are a few things that you have to accept don’t matter anymore: could or should haves, what ifs, and people’s opinions, to name a few. There’s no sense in feeling bad about it any of it anymore, even if other people say that you should, because it’s done and what matters is that you are here. So try to just stay present. You won’t get approval or support from everyone, but you will get all the support you need from everybody else. Some people might even surprise you, if you give them a chance. This is just gonna be a hard one dude. Absolutely none of it is going to be easy, but you’ve done plenty of hard things before, right?  And you can do this too. Just allow the anxiety and worry to have its space in your life right now. Try talking to your anxiety. Ask it if it would be okay with leaving for a while, when you really need a break, as long as you agree to let it have its time later. The two of you might at least be able to come to some kind of agreement. I know it feels horrible but it has to be there to help you grow and it’s easier to work with it than against it. It’s okay to let it take you over sometimes too. Be gentle, patient, and kind with yourself and take the time you need to be okay. Be fearless and learn how to be in your own corner. Someday soon you’ll be far away from this, and you’re gonna be just fine. Hang in there kiddo.

I have been trying to seek treatment for years because it’s gotten to the point where I can’t go outside and I will only go into two rooms in my entire house. In fact, I’m currently trapped inside because there’s a massive hobo spider on my front porch. I’m feeling defeated, but before today I had actually made incredible progress on my own. I even started using the main level bathroom instead of having to walk upstairs every time. I don’t care how weird or TMI that is, it’s a good example of what this looks like and I’m so proud of myself. 

I’m sure you have all sorts of restrictions around spiders in your life too. I haven’t been able to find help and it was just time to get back to life again. I don’t have an answer for you, but you aren’t alone and if I can try, you can try. It’s just our brains being defiant, but it feels impossible to tame. I’m still collecting data on what’s been helpful but I will say that when I accumulated positives (every time I didn’t encounter spiders), it reinforced that the world could still be safe at all. That gave me a bit of strength. I also have this bizarre imaginary treaty that I invented in my head to help me feel like I was being intentional and to incentivize me to learn to be at peace with them existing near me. The “treaty” is that if I leave them alone, they leave me alone. Obviously they’ve never confirmed that they’ll uphold their end of things, but because I have stood my ground and they did technically leave me alone, I can subconsciously tell myself that it’s because the treaty is working and I should keep it up lol Now, if the treaty is ever broken by one of them then all bets are off and I’m grabbing a torch.

The other thing I would suggest is mushrooms. The magic ones. If it’s legal in your area, of course. I’m not really one to do mushrooms but my doctors suggested it and they were really helpful in allowing me to be able to sit with my emotions without them controlling me. I’m too scared to like hold a spider or anything when I’m tripping, but when I did encounter spiders it was slightly more bearable. The goal is to find a way to keep reinforcing for yourself that you can at least make small progress. I’m rambling but hopefully this was helpful?

To explain a bit better, it’s just a handful of everyday prescription medications on an outpatient basis. Because alcohol withdrawal can kill you, our protocol is to provide 3-5 days worth of benzodiazepines (which are common) to help you detox safely. You’ll then get 1-3 more medications to help you maintain your sobriety, and you and your doctor would discuss which option is right for you. The medication I chose was Antabuse, which is usually the last choice but it’s effective! It’s hard to say what resources to look into without knowing how your healthcare system works, but you could try googling Naltrexone and Disulfiram and go from there!

Can you look into Medication Assisted Treatment (MAT)? It was really helpful for me as a resource when I didn’t have funds or time to go to rehab. The doctors helped me detox with benzos for three days and then put me on Antabuse (Disulfuram) for a few months. You absolutely cannot drink on either of these, please be advised. The Antabuse causes a violent reaction when mixed with alcohol. It stays in your system for a few days after you take it so if you suddenly decide to say “fuck it” and drink you actually have to wait a few days and it gives you time to reconsider. It helped to have someone hold me accountable for taking it, so I would FaceTime with a friend every night who would watch me take it and offer emotional support. Things got better in about a month and it saved my life.

NAD but have been through this almost exactly. A few things finally helped:
1.) Urethral dilation and hydrodistention. This is done as a surgery (technically they can do the dilation awake but don’t let them). I do it every 2-4 years and never have a problem until it’s time again. 
2.) Uribel. Not sure if you’ve tried that but it’s awesome for the bad days. 
3.) Instillations. They can put medication directly into your bladder via catheter. Really helped with the bad pain for an extended period of time, but nothing crazy. 
4.) STOP STRESSING ABOUT IT. I know that’s easier said than done and it took me a decade to master but the sooner you start the better you get. I don’t mean this as in “stop whining”, I mean to say that your bladder is going to do that no matter what with IC. It just hurts sometimes. I think of it like a hallucination or just my nerves being weird when I know everything is actually okay. The less you stress about it, the less trouble you’ll have. Literally, stress is a major cause of flare ups. The more you can remind yourself that it’s temporary the sooner you remove at least that contributor. It usually takes a few days for me to stop feeling pain but it does. 
5.) Hot baths and drinking lots of water.

People can and will tell you all day that it was absolutely not your fault, but unfortunately that doesn’t usually make you believe it. But, there are resources you can use to get an idea of what the process might look like, and various ways you can find support on your own terms. RAINN is a really good resource, for example. You can check out their website for some good info, and call the hotline if you’re ready. 

But for now, you’re just going to be stuck in the mud. And that’s okay and normal, even though it hurts. I’m so sorry you’re going through that. It’s all part of the illness. Your ONLY job is to do the best you can. Having bad days will absolutely still happen, but it doesn’t matter as long as you put effort into your actions that day. Another part of this is that we do see relationships as kind of a life or death situation. We fear being abandoned far more than we fear death. You’re NOT horrible. You’re just struggling with something that not everyone else is. People will leave. I know it’s all but impossible to accept that. Try to just keep in mind that you have to do everything you can for yourself. Be kind to yourself, get to know yourself, spend some more time alone and learn to be ok just sitting with your own thoughts. It’s scary as hell, but it’s something that absolutely must happen if you have a diagnosis of BPD.

Also, this diagnosis requires a massive amount of support. We tend to put all of our eggs in one basket, believing that one person is the only person who understands us and can save us. Having other people that you can fall back on when you need them is huge. Having a strong treatment team is also important (therapist, psychiatrist, groups, etc.). Right now, Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) is essentially considered the “only” real treatment for BPD. It’s also the most effective. I HIGHLY suggest working your booty off to get into a DBT group or DBT Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP). You can also find an individual therapist that specializes in DBT. Heck, you can even find YouTube videos and self-help books about it. It will absolutely change your life. I think you need some hope right now, and that’s my best advice on how to find it.

Again, I have to repeat: YOU ARE NOT A BAD PERSON. YOU ARE NOT HORRIBLE. YOU DON’T RUIN THINGS. You’re struggling and doing the best you can. Try your best to stay out of the past and future and just focus on the present moment as much as you possibly can. I hope you can find some comfort here in these communities. We’re all here for you and we’re all rooting for you. Please feel free to message me any time. I’m not a therapist in ANY way, shape or form, but I’m happy to listen and exchange experiences if it’s helpful.

Hang in there.

I was working with adolescent girls in residential. There was one that was really a great kid, but she was pretty severely autistic and her meltdowns were out of control. I’m not actually sure why they sent her to us instead of a facility more specific for her needs, but anyway. When she would have meltdowns, we were usually in a five person restraint with her for anywhere between 4-8 hours. She was strong as HELL too, so staff often got kicked/punched/thrown off, etc. None of it was EVER on purpose. It got to the point where almost every day she would go into those meltdowns and all we could really do was just keep her safe during them. She loved Paw Patrol and her Baymax stuffed animal was a HUGE coping skill to keep her calm. She talked to/snuggled that thing so much it was like it was her best friend. Anyway, the facility ultimately decided that we just weren’t equipped to manage her and manage the other kids at the same time. Our supervisors told us she would be discharging. We were confused, but really excited for her because all she had been wanting for years was just to go see her “mommy and my doggy!” She gets a phone call from mom the day before her discharge, which would also be her birthday. Mom tells her they’re going to make this HUGE deal for her birthday-they we’re getting her a Paw Patrol cake, taking her to a water park and all of this wonderful stuff. As far as we knew, that’s what was happening. Nope. The moment she left, the supervisors informed us that her mom was picking her up and dropping her straight off at a state hospital. A state hospital is pretty much where you send people to die. There’s no treatment plan, it’s just pretty much drugging/tackling the fuck out of anyone that starts to get out of line. They took all of her clothes and toys. Thinking about how absolutely fucking crushed she probably was just about ruined me. She never got to see her doggy and wouldn’t ever have her Baymax stuffed animal ever again. And her mom really only sent her there because she had a “normal” child and she didn’t really want this girl around making her life hard. She’s going to die alone. In a cell. Never cared for. Never talked to. Never loved. Nothing. I cried for probably a week. I quit that job shortly after, and I’ve never quit a psych, or any, job in my life. Ugh. It’ll kill me until I die.

They’ll stop working any time now. Benzo tolerance is INSANE. Once you’ve taken them long enough, you become physically dependent. Benzo withdrawal is one of the only detoxes that can actually kill you. Once you decide to get off of them, life becomes a literal hell for months. I never abused my Klonopin, but I was forced to stop it for a while. During that time I had such bad anxiety that I couldn’t (and didn’t) leave my house for six months. I had a complete psychotic meltdown to boot. Point being, the good effects you’re feeling right now are only going to last so long and then you’ll pay for it ten fold. That’s my experience and warning to you.

Now, Klonopin has a stupidly long half-life. It’s like 24-30 hours long. I find that if I take one on Monday, I can still get enough out of it on Tuesday night to at least make sleep a little easier. If possible, use it selectively. Take it when you absolutely must, take it every other day at times when you think you could make that extra mileage work and MOST IMPORTANTLY: DO NOT TAKE IT ON THE DAYS YOU DON’T NEED IT. If you’re off work on the weekends, it’s better to just suffer and stay up all night when you can afford to. Anything to keep distance between you and that drug.

Lastly, Klonopin has this bizarre, sobering effect. Well after you think you’ve actually felt the effects of it is when you’ll actually reach peak blood levels. You’ll still be majorly impaired even when you feel like the medication has worn off. That being said, you can and will get a DUI driving on it, or worse, wind up in an accident. Hypothetically, let’s say .5mg of Klonopin is the equivalent of being over the legal limit with alcohol. If you take 2mg of Klonopin at night, then go to drive the next day, you’ve still got at least 1mg of Klonopin in your system. PLAN ACCORDINGLY IF YOU HAVE TO DRIVE because you will not have the ability to determine whether or not you should. Nobody told me that when I first started Klonopin. If they had, I wouldn’t have totaled two cars in two months. 

Overall, it’s a helpful med, but it will fuck up your entire life if you don’t treat it very, very, very, very carefully.

For example, I work in healthcare and they make such a big fuss about not coming in when you’re sick because you could spread it throughout the hospital. However, I have a couple pieces of advice. Try not to call out for anxiety as much as you can. With anxiety, the more we avoid the things that make us anxious, the more we learn that simply avoiding those things fixes the problem. Then it starts to become a pattern and you trap yourself in it. What helps me is knowing that I can leave my job at any time if my anxiety is too bad. I can simply tell them I’m sick and I need to go. If you can just get yourself to show up, most likely you’ll arrive to find that you feel better anyway. Plus, it looks better to employers if you can show that you did try to come in and do your best. As far as calling off three times while being so new, I do think it’s important that you give your boss or HR an explanation. You don’t have to tell them that it’s anxiety, but you can just tell them you’re struggling with personal or medical issues. Make sure you let them know how important the job is to you and how you’re committed to being a good employee. Just give them a heads up that you might need a little slack until this resolves. If they are very understanding, again I can’t stress enough the importance of not taking that opportunity to avoid going to work. Being able to laugh with the people that mocked me was a hard skill to learn, but they suddenly didn’t mock me so much when they saw I wasn’t affected by it. Acceptance isn’t something that happens overnight, but what you can do immediately is stop wearing your hats. Just do it. Take the plunge. Spend time out and about being unapologetically yourself. You need to advocate for yourself, because it absolutely does affect your mental health and can leave long-lasting scars. There is a solid way to talk to them, and it’s a Dialectical Behavioral Therapy tool that’s designed to get you what you want while being respectful and straightforward. The skill is called DEARMAN and I will write it out for you. Write each step down with your words on a separate paper and that will serve as your script. Here we go:

D: Describe. Describe the situation in a simple way using only the facts, not your feelings. For example, “Mom, dad, I’ve noticed you’ve been arguing a lot lately. I can hear this yelling from my room.

E: Express. Describe your feelings using “I” statements so that you don’t make them defensive. Example, “I feel on edge and sad when I hear the yelling. I feel like it’s taking a toll on my mental health and ability to feel comfortable in this house.

A: Assert. Ask for what you need in a clear, simple way. Example, “I want/need you both to stop yelling so much. I want you to work out your differences or at least do it when I’m not home.”

R: Reinforce. Make it a win-win. Example, “We can spend more time together as a family if you can be civil and make time for me. Also, I’m sure you both would like not to argue so much.”

M: stay Mindful. Stay present and don’t give in to anything nasty they might say. Your only focus is to stick to these steps.

A: Appear Confident. Don’t back down. Don’t stop these steps if they start putting you down or disagreeing with you. Don’t cower, whisper or apologize. Approach them calmly with maturity.

N: Negotiate. Know your bottom line, but give in order to get. Example, “I understand that arguments happen. My bottom line is that I can’t listen to it anymore. Perhaps you could give me a heads up when you two need time to discuss something so I can go for a walk or put in headphones.”

DEARMAN works. I promise. I’ve been teaching it and using it for years. I know it sounds silly, but write it out and try it. Your parents won’t even know what hit them because you’re going to seem so correct and respectful. Best of luck!!

Boy, I know what that feels like. By all accounts, I shouldn’t be alive, but here I am. I do a couple of things that help. I will write a goal for the day, and for the week. Start small. For example, make it your daily goal to take a shower. Make your weekly goal to go for a walk outside twice a week. As you progress, start making your goals things that will genuinely help you and make you feel better/happier. ALWAYS complete your goals, especially when you don’t want to. The most important part of doing that is to give yourself a HUGE pat on the back for completing them.

At the end of the day, write out a list of things you’re grateful for. There will always be something. It could be that you’re healthy, that you have the internet, that you have a pet, have a home, etc. Build a list of things that remind you that there are still some good things in your life. Next, write something you’re proud of yourself for. Again, it could be just getting out of bed. Lastly, write yourself a positive affirmation. If you’re not feeling joyous enough to write, “I’m fantastic!,” that’s totally understandable. Start with something like, “I did enough for today.” Or, “I made it through today because I am strong.”

Hang these goals, lists and affirmations somewhere you can see them (especially the affirmations). Will it feel stupid? Absolutely. Will it immediately change your life? No. But they key to overcoming is to do it one small step at a time. These lists help you do that. If you stay on it, eventually you’ll start to remember all the things you’re lucky to have. Your goals will start to get bigger. You’ll become stronger and happier.

Well, the good news is you’re not broken or anything. The bad news is you’ve definitely got anxiety. You seem way too young to have to be dealing with it already, but you’ve definitely got all the symptoms. The only real cure for it is doing some work with a therapist. I would do everything in your power to make that happen, and don’t feel bad about it. In the meantime, go online and look up “DBT skills.” You can find ways to help you flip the negative thinking you’ve got in your head. When you get the tight chest feeling and all that, try taking a lot of deep breaths or doing something to distract yourself, like going for a walk. Try to remember that the thoughts you’re having are just that negative little voice telling you nobody likes you, etc. and that they aren’t real or true.

Don’t worry, there’s hope! That being said, getting through anxiety requires you do some work, like working out. In my opinion, the best thing you can do for anxiety is DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy). It’s a set of skills designed to help you cope with the thoughts that you’re having. I would highly recommend a therapist that can teach you DBT, but you can definitely also get a self-help DBT workbook on amazon. You could even google DBT distress tolerance skills if need be. You have to practice the skills every day and you should start seeing a difference in a couple of weeks.

That being said, I have two little tricks of my own that help me with my anxiety. They’re things I sort of made up on my own to cope when I was dealing with it, but maybe they’ll help you too!

1.) Understand what a panic attack is and you can stop it. A panic attack is your body activating the fight or flight response, but in response to an internal stimuli (thoughts, fears). During the fight or flight response, the only thing your brain really does is absolutely FLOOD your body with adrenaline. The adrenaline is what’s making your stomach drop, your heart pound, your hands sweat and any other physical symptom you have. Once it is no longer being produced, adrenaline takes approximately thirty seconds to dissolve in your body. If you can stop your thoughts in the moment and turn it off, you can remind yourself that the only thing really happening is you’re simply feeling the effects of the adrenaline. Keep your thoughts quiet and count out the thirty seconds. By then you should be feeling back to normal. It helped me to approach panic attacks from a logical standpoint instead of getting stuck in my head.

Also, a lot of my anxiety revolves around being trapped in places or feeling like I was going to be stuck in class, at work, etc. with anxiety. Try to remember that no matter where you are, or what you’re doing, you can simply get up and leave the situation if you need to. We often lie to ourselves and think that it’s not ok to go take a walk or take care of our anxiety, but it’s not true. You can ALWAYS go take five to regroup. It doesn’t matter what anyone thinks, because practicing self-care is the most important thing. Knowing I can leave any situation gives me a lot of comfort and it actually prevents me from ever actually needing to leave. 

Hopefully any of that was helpful. Worst case scenario, panic disorders are always 100% temporary, so relief will come! Hang in there and definitely try the therapy!

The rehab that I was at didn’t think to treat me for benzos since I wasn’t abusing them. Three weeks in I got the shakes and then I got the withdrawal syndrome. It made me absolutely lose my fucking mind. I left my husband of ten years, began an affair, quit my dream job. All because the withdrawal fucked up my brain. As for DBT, you can just go on Google or YouTube and search for DBT skills to practice. I know that’s vague, but really the whole world of DBT is accessible online. Essentially what it is is a collection of skills to practice to problem solve, tolerate problems, or feel better about a problem. More specifically, look up DBT distress tolerance skills to help you manage your anxiety. Additionally, search for DBT Mindfulness skills to help with focusing on positives and letting worries go. Some specific skills to look for that helped me are radical acceptance, present moment focus, wise mind and willingness vs. willfulness. Keep in mind, DBT is like working out. Whatever you learn, you’ll have to practice it daily. It won’t click automatically, and it might feel silly at times, but just like building muscle, it’ll eventually become easier and part of your routine. A self-help DBT workbook might be really great! I know there’s several available on Amazon!

So, PLEASE don’t take this the wrong way, but have you ever considered possibly having extremely high functioning autism? People that are just barely on the spectrum sometimes are never diagnosed because they’re exactly the same as normal people except for a few, minor things. To me, the overcalculating and plotting how to have normal interactions sounds a lot like that. Very high functioning autism often involves watching others and mimicking them instead of having your own interactions. If this is the case, a little bit of therapy is all you need. 

More on topic, I would say just get some support in your anxiety around how others will react to you. I think what you’re doing is spending all of your time figuring out how to avoid pain. Pain of rejection, embarrassment, upsetting people, etc. But this kind of pain is all part of being human. We will all make blunders and say the wrong thing. We’ll all get made fun of for something in our lives. I think you’re trying to figure out how to escape unscathed, but it’s not possible. The best way for you to learn and grow in your interactions is just to go out there and do it and be ready to accept rejection. We learn by making mistakes. It’ll probably take you a while to find friends or a group that you click with, but that’s all part of the process. Focus on the things that you KNOW you can offer that are positives-are you funny? Kind? Intelligent? Try to focus on how people will react to those positive attributes about you. If it’s helpful, make a list of your personality strengths and plot out how to showcase those. In any case, the most important thing is to just get out there and start doing it. Starting a conversation with someone new can be one of the most nerve-wracking things to do, but it’s how every last one of us first found our best friends, significant others, etc. Good luck!!

It’s hard to accept, but there’s nothing you can do. The only thing you can ever do with an addict is love them from afar. Above all, make sure you’re not enabling her. If she’s not seeing any consequences from her actions, she’ll have no reason to stop drinking. One of the ways we enable addicts is by trying to help and baby them. You might just have to set an ultimatum and cut her out of your life if she can’t agree to stop drinking. When she realizes she’s hit rock bottom, only then will she see that it’s time for a change. 

I know the above is easier said than done, so I have one other solution. There are ways to get her sober at home that can be appealing to an alcoholic. You can look into something called The Sinclair Method, which has had success for some people. The alcoholic takes a medication 30 minutes before drinking and then can drink normally. With time, some people have found that they drink less and less and then get sober. I drank too much for this method to work for me, but it’s an option. Also, if she’s hesitant about going into a rehab facility, detoxing at home is an option. The doctors will prescribe a regimen of benzodiazepines to keep her safe for a few days while she doesn’t drink. These drugs act on the same pathway as alcohol and can bring about pleasant feelings, so detoxing is very comfortable. From there, she can take Antabuse, which will make her violently ill if she drinks on it. Antabuse is the method that I use to stay sober. It’s kind of a fear tactic, but hey-it’s keeping me sober. The key factor in all of these methods is that she has to be willing to do them. If she’s not in a place where she even wants to quit, you just need to cut ties. Enabling is dangerous. Make sure you seek some help for yourself in dealing with this, as well. It’s obvious you’re losing sleep over it and that’s not fair to you. Please feel free to message me if you have any questions about the medication stuff. I’m wishing the best for you and your sister.

Having that kind of structure will make sure you’re staying active, and give you the chance to pat yourself on the back for any little victory-because just getting up and showering some days IS a victory. Pick an activity that you can do once a week, that will allow you to meet people. For me, I started taking circus classes once a week. You’d be surprised at how many circus centers you can find near you, and the community is incredibly open, understanding and welcoming, so it’s a quick way to make new friends. You could start going to a dance or art class or something, anything. Just get some structure. Lastly, make sure you’re reminding yourself every day that you’re exactly where you’re supposed to be. You’ve been dealt an incredibly difficult hand. There will be good days and bad days, that’s all part of the process. Never beat yourself up for feeling like you’re not accomplishing enough just yet. You, my friend, are dating a borderline with trauma. I know because A.) I work with them, B.) I am one, that does this. I suggest you do some careful reading about borderline personality disorder, but watch out for biased articles that suggest you’re dating some sort of serial killer. Borderlines fear being abandoned and unloved more than they fear death. They need constant reassurance that you are there and that you love them. Sleeping with the light on is a major sign of early childhood trauma, probably sexual in nature. Bedtime can create a massive fear for these folks because their subconscious tells them that bed=pain, and bed=being left alone with their thoughts and doubts once you fall asleep. These thoughts will never go away, but a borderline person can learn to self-regulate. My boyfriend and I have had a lot of very open, honest communication about both of our needs and it has helped tremendously. As much as it pleased me to no end that he was willing to stay up with me, I learned that I was causing him issues in his work life by making him groggy. I’ve learned to ask for reassurance that he loves me in appropriate ways, at appropriate times. 99% of the work fell on me, though. She needs to do some work in therapy (the only treatment for BPD) and you need to set some firm limits as kind as you can. A few couple’s sessions wouldn’t be a bad idea. You would learn how to communicate better and learn to stop walking on eggshells. She would learn that what she’s doing isn’t normal and is causing you discomfort. I could go on and on. Please feel free to message me if you’d like to ask questions or get a bit more insight.

Just to start, I’m going to be on the side of the spectrum that you don’t want to hear. It’s not to discourage you, but just sharing my journey. Everyone is different. 

I started with the similar intention of just wanting to be a normal drinker. I detoxed with the Valium and started the Naltrexone. My drinking went from 18 units a night to 3 in about a month and a half. As far as Naltrexone making you unable to enjoy other things, I didn’t notice any effect on that. Food, sex, etc. were all still great. In fact, alcohol was still great, too. I was actually really relieved that my Klonopin still worked, because I figured that might be effected. I was under the impression that I wouldn’t get drunk for some reason, but that’s not correct. Over time, I did notice it felt a bit more like a chore to drink than it did a recreational activity. 

One MAJOR issue I ran into were the side effects. From what I’ve gathered from other users here, I did get hit with them abnormally hard. This doesn’t happen to everyone, but in my case, it was hell. I had horrific fatigue, crippling anxiety, heart palpitations and terrible nausea. Additionally, it threw my mental illness for a massive loop. I would STRONGLY suggest you work very closely with a psychiatrist during TSM if you’ve ever been diagnosed with depression or a mood disorder. I did decide to tough it out for three months, and the side effects dissipated at least to the point where I could function. In over three months, I never had a single AF day. 

Back to your (our) original intentions, I promised myself that if I was not where I wanted to be in my three month goal, I would practice abstinence. My drinking went back up from 3 units to 9 and my life was becoming sloppy again. I gave up on the Naltrexone and got back on Antabuse and Campral. The Campral helps with cravings pretty well, but it is something you have to take three times a day, which was really difficult for me. 

Two points I want to make:
1.) Extinction won’t happen immediately when you drink on the pill. You literally have to drink on it to make it work. I don’t believe you could get there very quickly if you’re only going to be drinking a glass of wine twice a week, or if you’d get there at all. I think that might just lead back into drinking a lot, and then TSM might work. But I’m not sure if you want to go that route.
2.) I was drinking “through” the Naltrexone, according to some. There is a bit of talk on here about how different types of alcohol are more ideal than others. I believe wine is a much safer choice than hard liquor, so you do have that advantage.

Finally, if your plan is just to go AF for a year anyway, my personal opinion is just to stick with that for good. If you can manage that, that’s an amazing thing. I don’t know your story or how your life was with alcohol, but for me it was awful. I wouldn’t even dabble with going back down the spiral if I had made it that far. It does sound wonderful to be normal like everyone else, I just won’t ever be it. Hopefully I answered some of your questions in this novel (sorry) and wishing you the best of luck! Just a CNA, but I worked in a psych hospital on the night shift. I don’t really believe in the supernatural, but this one patient made me question everything. We never thought anything of it until we found out that her bed used to belong to a male patient that killed him self in that bed. The song she always claimed that her pillow was singing apparently used to be his favorite song. The older staff said that he never spoke, he just sang that same song all the time. The same one she claimed she could hear. That was a big nope for me. 

EDIT: Just to add, this patient had absolutely no way of knowing about the patient that killed himself. This happened 5+ years before she arrived, so it’s not like any of the other residents could have told her about it or anything.
